RAG is officially cooked.

IBM built a retriever that hallucinates 65x less than fine-tuned RAG systems.

Right now, every company is using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to stop their AI from hallucinating.

The idea is to give the AI a private database to read so it doesn't make things up.

But there is a massive structural flaw.

Standard RAG blindly grabs documents based on vector similarity and forces the AI to read them. If the retriever pulls irrelevant garbage, the AI doesn't stop.

It just hallucinates with citations.

IBM just dropped a paper that changes the math entirely.

They built a new retrieval architecture that hallucinates 65x less than state-of-the-art fine-tuned RAG systems.

65x is the difference between a fun prototype and a production-grade enterprise system.

Instead of blindly dumping context into the model and hoping for the best, their system actively filters and validates the retrieved data before the generation step even begins.

It cuts out the noise. It forces absolute precision.

For businesses, this is the holy grail.

Zero hallucinations means zero liability. It means autonomous agents can finally be trusted with sensitive company data without a human babysitting every output.

The guy who helped make The Land Before Time walked out of Disney in 1979 because he thought they were cheaping out on the drawings.

Prada just hired him to hand-draw its Christmas ads. They even left his messy pencil sketches in the final photos.

His name is John Pomeroy, and he started at Disney back in 1973. On September 13, 1979, he quit with Don Bluth and Gary Goldman right in the middle of making The Fox and the Hound. Their complaint was that the studio kept trimming the expensive detail work to save money. So they went off and started their own studio, with about $200,000 of equipment they paid for themselves. Around a quarter of Disney's animation department followed them out the door, and The Fox and the Hound got pushed back six months.

That little rebel studio went on to make The Secret of NIMH, Dragon's Lair, An American Tail and The Land Before Time.

Pomeroy came back to Disney in the 90s to lead the animation on John Smith in Pocahontas. Then he left again in 2003, when Disney shut down hand-drawn animation.

Now look at what Coca-Cola did last Christmas. It made its holiday ad with AI and bragged about it. Coke said five people sorted through 70,000 AI clips and finished in about a month, when these ads used to take a year.

Coke was probably right to do it. People online hated the ad, but when System1 tested it on regular viewers it scored 5.9 out of 6. If you sell soda in 140 countries, you want something cheap that feels like Christmas, and most people grabbing a Coke don't care how the polar bear got made.

Prada sells something else entirely. When you buy a Prada bag, a big part of what you're paying for is knowing somebody spent way more than they needed to. Luxury has always worked like this. Before the sewing machine, nobody paid extra for a hand-stitched shirt, because every shirt was hand-stitched. Hand-stitching only got expensive once machines made it rare.

AI is doing the same thing to pictures right now. Anybody can type a prompt and get a snowy forest with a cute fox in a couple of minutes. So a fox somebody actually drew, at roughly 12 drawings for every second of film, is suddenly worth a lot more. Those pencil sketches sitting behind the actors are Prada showing you the receipt.

There's a hand-drawn fox walking through the snow in this campaign. Pomeroy quit Disney 47 years ago in the middle of a fox movie because he thought they were cutting corners on the drawings, and now Prada is paying him to draw a fox the slow way.

New essay:
https://t.co/Tm7eYpIXxs

NEW FOUNDER ARCHETYPES IN THE AI AGE

Solo founders
- Why: Solo founders can do 100x with AI, so they can ship a v1 when previously they couldn’t have before
- Why not: Maybe a team of cofounders still makes more progress. Maybe you can agentically code but someone still needs to do a million meetings with customers. Maybe coding was never the main bottleneck for startups in the first place?

Non-technical founders
- Why: There’s elite talent that comes from areas like finance, consulting, who can’t code but are passionate about business. There’s also folks in creative industries who create all day but just not in code. Now they can build
- Why not: Why not: Maybe AI makes it easier to build a prototype, but there’s still a big gap between a demo and a reliable product that can scale. If everyone can build the first version, maybe technical judgment becomes more important in deciding what to build, what’s actually possible, and how to stay ahead as the product gets more complex. (especially true for product categories like dev tools/etc)

Domain experts
- Why: A doctor who works at a hospital understands all the problems they face each day. A real estate broker really gets the subtleties of their markets, their clients. Same with a soldier, teacher, etc. What if they could use software to solve their own problems and build business along the way?
- Why not: Hoteliers didn’t create Airbnb and the finance industry didn’t create Kalshi. Sometimes you just need an outsider’s view in order to reinvent an industry, versus building incremental improvements

Kids, high schoolers, college students
- Why: Young people have already been building products early on. Start with a Minecraft mod, a Roblox game, a Discord bot, and suddenly you’ve learned how to make something that thousands of other people use. Now add AI, and a kid with an idea can build way more, way earlier
- Why not: Building something your friends love is very different from building a company. You still have to hire, raise money, manage people, and figure out how to make money. And maybe young founders have an advantage in consumer products because they understand their peers, but much less of one when it comes to enterprise software, healthcare, or other industries where experience and relationships really matter. Sometimes you just need domain expertise

Content creators
- Why: They’re already creating. So instead of creating videos, maybe the same skills can go into creating software. Plus, they have distribution. They know what their followers care about, how to get their attention, and how to reach them without paying for ads. In the past, turning that audience into a software product meant finding a technical cofounder or hiring a team. Now a creator could build and launch something themselves, and immediately put it in front of millions of potential users.
- Why not: Having followers helps with a spike of distribution, but building a sustainable growth engine is something else. The most valuable products aren’t memes - they are long-running, long-growing products that need to be endlessly tweaked and iterated on. Does the DNA work?

OpenAI just announced that its model proved the Standard Model of physics actually exists.

That sounds absurd. It's not.

For 70 years, physics has had a dirty secret.

Quantum field theory is the most accurate theory humanity has ever built. It predicts properties of the electron to more than 10 decimal places. The LHC, the Higgs boson, the chips in your phone all run on it.

And yet no mathematician had ever proven it exists.

Physicists have been using it like a recipe that works every single time, without anyone being able to prove the dish is a coherent object. We built cathedrals for 70 years on foundations nobody had verified.

The problem is so hard that in 2000 the Clay Institute made it one of its 7 Millennium Prize Problems, $1M each. In 26 years, only one has been solved (Poincaré, by Perelman, who refused the money).

Here's the timeline OpenAI just published:

September 9, 2026: their model produces a proof that Yang–Mills theory exists.
September 18: it extends it to QCD, the full theory of the strong force, with quarks.
Then to a completion of the Standard Model.
October 16: the Yang–Mills proof is formalized in Lean, meaning a machine checked every single logical step.
To understand why this is insane, you need to understand the problem.
Forget particles as tiny balls. The universe is made of invisible oceans stacked on top of each other: an electron field, a photon field, a gluon field. A particle is just a wave on one of those oceans.
But in quantum mechanics, the oceans are never calm. They ripple at every scale. Zoom in, you see smaller ripples. Zoom in again, smaller still. It never stops.

So when you do the math, those fluctuations add up to infinity.

Physicists found a trick called renormalization: subtract one infinity from another, and what's left matches experiment perfectly. It works. But mathematically it's duct tape. Nothing guaranteed there was a real object underneath.

Now the hardest case: Yang–Mills, the theory of gluons.

Gluons are the glue holding quarks together inside every atom in your body. And unlike light, they interact with each other. Two light beams pass through each other. Two gluons collide and stick. The field feeds on itself. That's what made it untameable.

The key that unlocks it won David Gross the 2004 Nobel Prize: asymptotic freedom.

The strong force gets weaker the closer you look. Think of a rubber band between two fingers. Close together, it's slack and the fingers move freely. Pull them apart, the tension explodes. That's why you never see a lone quark.

And that's the gift: the infinities come from tiny scales, and tiny scales are exactly where the theory goes calm. You zoom in, the monster falls asleep.

The method: turn spacetime into a grid, like pixels. On a grid, everything is finite. Then refine the grid, again and again, and prove the picture converges instead of exploding.

A mathematician named Balaban did a huge part of this in the 1980s and never finished. The construction sat open for 40 years. According to OpenAI, the AI closed it.

Now look at who's reviewing it.

David Gross, the Nobel laureate whose mechanism makes the proof work.
Arthur Jaffe, who literally wrote the Millennium Prize problem and co-founded the Clay Institute.
Plus Douglas, Klebanov, Nekrasov.

The man who wrote the question is now reading a machine's answer.

And in the same blog post, almost in passing: the Exponential Time Hypothesis in computer science is false, and the Kakeya conjecture is solved in every dimension.

Three bombs in one post.
Honest caveats, because they matter:
This is not the full Millennium Prize. The Clay problem has two parts: existence and the "mass gap". OpenAI claims existence only.
The physics materials aren't public yet. Gross's group chose to write it up themselves first.
Lean verifies the logic, but experts still have to confirm the formal statement really captures what physicists mean.
And it changes zero predictions. Physicists won't calculate anything differently tomorrow. It proves the ground under the cathedral is real.

But the craziest part isn't the theorem.

It's the scene.

Nobel laureates are now acting as interpreters of what a machine discovered. OpenAI calls its proofs "raw research data" and refuses academic credit.

For centuries, science worked one way: humans discover, then humans explain.

We may have just entered the era where machines discover, and humans explain.

Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, says AI should one day be priced by the value it creates: a few cents for telling someone to restart their Mac, maybe tens of millions for telling a drug company to move an aromatic ring to the other end of a molecule.

I understand the wish. I don't think the market will grant it.

I started in telecom in the 90s. Nobody ever paid us what a phone call was worth to them. The call that closed a deal and the call to say happy birthday cost the same, and the price was set by the next carrier willing to carry it for less.

AI is heading the same way. On Saturday Torsten Slok, the chief economist at Apollo, wrote that outside the big tech companies, corporate America is starting to treat token spending as a cost center that weighs on margins. Apollo also notes that demand is so price sensitive that it switches to cheap open-source models when prices go up even modestly.

The tens of millions from the better molecule go to whoever owns the molecule. If AI labs want to be paid for value, they will have to own the outcome: discover the drug, run the trial, hold the patent. That is why Isomorphic Labs, the drug discovery company Alphabet spun out of DeepMind, matters more than any pricing page.

Selling intelligence is becoming a commodity business. Owning what intelligence discovers is not.

2115413543764050165.text:
Back in 1985, barely anyone knew who Tommy Hilfiger was. So he bought a billboard in Times Square saying he was one of the four greatest designers in America, right next to Ralph Lauren, Perry Ellis and Calvin Klein. Twenty-five years later, the company that owned Calvin Klein paid $3 billion for him.

Somebody just put the same trick up on a billboard in San Francisco.

The Hilfiger sign was basically a game of hangman. It read "The 4 great American designers for men are" with blanks for each name and only the initials filled in, and down at the bottom in small type it admitted his logo belonged to the least known of the four.

He had almost no money for ads. George Lois, the ad guy his investor brought in, told him that if he marketed himself like every other fashion brand, it would take him 20 years to build a name. Tommy's first reaction to the hangman idea was that people would think he'd lost his mind, and he only said yes because he figured he had nothing to lose.

Think about what your brain does when you read that sign. You see three names you already think of as the best in the business, and you drop the fourth one into the same bucket before you ever stop to ask whether he belongs there. Hilfiger got filed next to Calvin Klein without proving a thing, because your brain did the filing for him.

Now look at the billboard sitting by the Bay Bridge on-ramp in San Francisco. It's five app icons floating in front of a giant moon, and that's the whole ad.

Four of those apps come from Anthropic, Perplexity, xAI and OpenAI. Add up what investors last paid for those companies and you get more than $2 trillion. (xAI, the company behind Grok, is part of SpaceX now.)

The one sitting in the middle is Notion, last valued at $11 billion. That's about half a percent of what everyone else on that sign is worth put together.

Notion has spent three years trying to get people to stop thinking of it as a notes app and start thinking of it as an AI company, and the business is getting there. Reports say AI plans were bringing in more than half its revenue by early this year, and Sacra estimates it hit $865 million in annual recurring revenue this summer, up 82% from a year ago. There's been IPO talk for months too, and Wall Street pays a lot more for every dollar an AI company brings in than it does for a notes app. Which bucket you put Notion in is worth billions of dollars to them.

Leaving the words off is the smartest part. If the sign said "Notion, the AI workspace," you'd roll your eyes and keep driving. With nothing written on it, the only thing left to think about is who made the row, which is exactly the question you want people asking about you.

Nobody's signed it, either. If that N in the middle turns out to be the one paying, it wouldn't be Notion's first mystery billboard. Back in July it put up "AI Dread?" signs around the city with nothing but a phone number on them, and only owned up after the SF Standard tracked it down.

It took Tommy 25 years to go from that billboard to a $3 billion check, and with an IPO on the table, Notion would very much like its version to pay off a lot sooner.

the most famous advice in YCombinator is 5 words long:

"do things that don't scale"

Paul Graham wrote it in 2013 and founders still get it wrong.

Most people read it as "be scrappy."

It actually means: recruit your first users by hand, one by one.

The examples are legendary:

→ Airbnb founders flew to New York, went door to door, and photographed hosts' apartments themselves.
→ The Collison brothers didn't send Stripe signup links. They'd say "let me set it up for you right now" and grab your laptop.

A message that proves you looked at who they are and what they just did.

Set it up yourself.

Send them a Loom of their own account configured.

Text them after the first week.
Ask what's broken.
Fix it before they ask twice.

Their words become your landing page, your cold emails, your pitch.

the talking shouldn't scale.

the finding can.

Don't automate the relationship.

Automate the search.

Vercel CI solves the "AI coding bottleneck" via:
① Fast and stable infrastructure (faster work)
② Turborepo integration (less work)
③ Agentic CI

① is obvious. Your CI is slow, flaky, goes down. We solve that. We operate 20 worldwide clusters doing millions of microVMs per day.

② is less obvious, but very powerful. Turborepo was designed to intelligently skip and cache prior work. The graph of dependencies is computed, not written. 

Ask your agent to migrate to @turborepo and start saving money and time. Even if you don't use us. But you should, it's really good.

③ is a game-changer. 𝚟𝚎𝚛𝚌𝚎𝚕 𝚌𝚒 in the CLI is the first step, because now your agents can inspect, abort, trigger, replay CI. Vercel Agent can help optimize it. And this is just the start.

You can expect a lot of hooks and capabilities to make CI something far more intelligent, that can even capture the nuance and judgment an engineer would have ("Are those tests even worth running?")

Agentic CI is the future of how we ship software. Excited to build it with you all!

New from ElevenLabs research: Today we’re sharing more about Cue, our new forced alignment model. It places every character on the audio timeline with more precision than any other aligner we tested. That means the right words show up at the right time.

Forced alignment is the step that turns a transcript into timestamps. It’s how subtitles land on time, how dubbed lines match the speaker, and how clicking a word in a transcript jumps to the moment it was said. Most open-source aligners are built for short, clean clips in a limited set of languages. Cue is one model that handles recordings of any length in a single pass. On real-world audio, it was more accurate than every open-source aligner we tested in all 29 languages of our benchmark. It aligns an hour of audio in about half a second on one GPU.

Cue already powers every Speech to Text transcription on ElevenLabs, and it’s available on its own through the Forced Alignment API.

2115554685352661369.text:
last night, yc f26 founders heard from @james406 from @posthog

one thing that he said resonated with me deeply: 

"being more ambitious can make a startup easier to build - not because the work gets easier, but because the idea gives customers, teammates, and investors something to get excited about."

the challenge is making progress on that ambition *this week*

james shared an analogy i loved: “elephant carpaccio.” instead of building the feet first and promising the rest of the elephant later, build a thin slice that shows the shape of the whole thing.

a few other lessons i'm taking away:

- put a product in people’s hands quickly. polite interest isn’t the same as usage.

- ask not just where your first customers came from, but why they came. then do more of what’s working.

- don’t mistake self-serve for no human touch. posthog saw 30-40 percentage points better NRR among customers it had regular relationships with. correlation isn’t causation, but the pattern was hard to ignore. customer success became a major hiring focus for them.

- be decisive enough to learn when you’re wrong. posthog pushed its “self-driving” positioning hard, then adjusted when users showed they wanted more composable tools.

Introducing Samaya Sterling, our new model post-trained for challenging financial research that outperforms the frontier! Sterling started off as a two person research effort to see if we could increase efficiency in agentic orchestration. To our surprise we were able to post-train a much smaller model (Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters) to greater accuracy (58.9% vs 55.9% on FrontierFinance) and 11x lower cost ($0.61 vs $6.89) than Claude Fable 5.1, the best performing frontier model.

We did this via a four-stage training process, two stages of SFT where the model first learns to research with our financial tools and how to construct a good agentic research strategy. The second two stages are RL, with an offline GRPO stage where the model further hones its research strategy from eight teachers that provide diverse approaches, and an online GRPO stage where the model can make end to end attempts and learn from its mistakes.

We see substantial gains from the co-adaptation of the model and harness through post-training, both through the model learning to effectively use the high-quality financial tools, and better compaction approaches that let even a small model execute on longer and deeper research.

We are exploring multiple follow-up directions, from multi-agent research swarms using this small model, to training firm-specific models to encode unique judgement, to training a larger model, where early results show even greater gains from the training process.

The full research is linked below!

Oracle now targets at least $30B in free cash flow for fiscal 2029, when investors expected negative cash.

Oracle burned $23.7B of free cash flow in fiscal 2026 building AI data centers for OpenAI and others, and plans $90B to $95B of capex this year.

In September, CFO Hilary Maxson refused to say when that drain would end; At Investor Day today she put the turn in the second half of fiscal 2028.

The plan depends on capital spending peaking in fiscal 2027 and 2028, then stepping down as new capacity starts earning revenue.

Oracle also capped further capital raising through fiscal 2030 at $20B, split evenly between equity and gross debt, beyond a $20B share sale it already completed.

Way back in the day (i.e. like late 2025-early 2026) I used to do a bit whenever I was on a panel with @neil_chilson or @KevinTFrazier or whoever where if they brought up the "patchwork of state laws" thing I would point out that the few existing state AI safety laws were very light touch and harmonized, and I would accuse the interlocutor of being a "regulatory doomer" because they were concerned about speculative future harms from state AI laws. Great bit, always killed. People love the "regulatory doomer" line. 

I don't think I can really do it any more, though, because it kind of seems like states really are about to pass a bunch of very different laws, some of which do in fact impose obligations on frontier AI developers.

I'm not saying that's a bad thing, to be clear; I don't think the current level of regulation (essentially zero) is anywhere near defensible, and since Congress isn't ready to get serious about federal legislation states should and will get to work and start trying out different things. But it is funny to me that all of the doomers are being proven right at the same time.

Tech/IT Layoffs: A Survivors' Guide

AI-led layoff tsunami is real. Microsoft, Amazon, Meta have begun. Others will follow. AI has infinite payoff. Tech workers are an inefficient cost burden. Capitalism will get rid of you. Jungle Rules for Survival:.

You Are Your Only Friend

1. Be Self-Serving: Your employer pays for skills, not loyalty. Your employment relationship is merely a transaction, lasting only till it improves shareholder returns. The moment AI produces better ROI, your usefulness is over.

2. Stay Ruthlessly Prepared: Treat your job like a one-client business. Update your skills aggressively. Build your personal brand online. Create a strong network. Engage with ex-colleagues & recruiters when you don’t have to.

3. Know Your Exit Math: Read your contract: notice period, severance, RSU vesting, non-compete and moonlighting clauses. Don’t “resign” under pressure in a layoff. Don’t trust verbal assurances. Don’t sign release documents until you know what you are owed.

4. Keep a Private Log: Maintain notes of each project impact, each bottleneck resolution, each outcome. Record measurable gains in revenue, cost savings, and error reduction. Numbers have power. In a layoff, your records will be your edge for the next job.

5. Think the Unthinkable: Assume your access can be disabled tomorrow 6:00 am. Keep personal contacts, portfolio, tax docs, and other pvt info outside company systems. The day you're laid off: get into war mode, mobilize your network, and message 20 people.

6. Search While Employed: Don’t resign without an offer in hand. If there is no skill upgrade happening in your current role, find a new job before your skills become outdated. Do 2-4 job interviews every quarter even if you’re happy (but stagnant).

7. Be Market-Relevant: Keep reinventing yourself. Stay ahead of the curve. Master all three layers: (a) Base layer (b) AI layer (c) Domain layer. Set aside at least 1 hr/day for skills upgrade. Two demonstrable projects are better than 12 certifications.

8. Respect Your Identity: You are not your job title. AI does not reward overwork. It rewards high-leverage individuals. Divide your worries into “controllable” (skills, savings, health) and “uncontrollable” (unrealistic deadlines, stress at workplace). Focus only on the first list.

Endquote: Survival of the Fittest

Every morning in the jungles of Africa, a deer wakes up knowing it must run faster than the fastest lion, and the lion knows it must run faster than the slowest deer in order to survive.

The law of the tech jungle is no different: Run faster than others, or die.

2115548060499714265.text:
I don’t think people realize how selfless and wonderful the StackOverflow’s founders were.

Unlike reddit, x etc they insisted ALL of their content will be 100% open, nothing will ever be locked up in walled garden. 

They made it a point by even offering structured data downloads! 

They didn’t cared people cloning the website. They didn’t worry about putting the whole monetization thing at risk.

It was a true hacker spirit in it’s purest form.

Most folks won’t be able to grasp how hard this is. You are on top of the world. Millions of people depend on you daily. You have the rarest opportunity to rack in billions. And you still stay true to your principles.

This exactly in turn later enabled AI revolution. I still remember downloading entire SO archives and preparing it for pre-training while Reddit and others went onto lawfare and firewalling the content. Note that this was the content their users - not reddit employees - had created for free and voluntarily to help others and the world. But they locked it all up for profiting from it personally.

SO did none of that. I think they knew they will be sacrificed at the altar. Yet it will exactly serve the intent of their founding principles to help others and the world, now through AI, even at bigger scale.

All of today’s models are built upon efforts of such true pure hackers who spent their days and years to create training data for AIs. I was a proud SO contributer for many years and there are couple of times while testing models I did felt that models might have used my answers 😇.

Hats off to @codinghorror and @spolsky and so many builders and hackers at SO for moving the world forward, one revolution at a time 🫡.

Companies don't necessarily need bigger marketing budgets. They need someone who knows exactly what to do with the resources they already have.

SF Compute CEO @evanjconrad explains why GPU clusters are bad collateral for lenders:

"This article was more of a prediction of a trend that is already happening. I probably should’ve said, currently, most startups cannot buy compute. It is only getting harder and harder and harder."

"If you want to finance a GPU cluster, you need to first have collateral, which is typically the hardware itself. The problem with that collateral is nobody wants to buy the hardware. They want to buy the hardware in a data center that’s operated by a company that works."

"And the situation in which you recoup that hardware is often the situation in which the person operating that hardware is just as likely to blow up. There’s a lot of correlated risk."

"If you are the startup trying to buy a cluster, to the eyes of a lender, you look like you’re gonna blow up."

Two companies he had poured his heart, soul, and everything he had into were on the brink of collapse. He had just $30 to $40 million left, and saving one meant risking the life of the other

Nearly two decades later, Tesla has transformed the electric vehicle industry, and SpaceX has revolutionized spaceflight

2115497113664754104.text:
It's confusing why a major multi billion dollar law firm is going bankrupt.

So I talked to a bunch of lawyer friends about why Weil could suddenly be insolvent.

Unintuitively, law firms are basically fixed-cost businesses. Revenue comes from a concentrated core group of rainmakers.

Those rainmakers carry the whole business, while the rest of the business basically drags ass. Junior partners are rainmakers-in-training--they can't yet bring in the huge load-bearing dollars.

Everyone else--associates, back office staff--comprises one gigantic fixed cost center. Not to mention basic overhead like offices, revolver interest (for cashflow timing needs), etc.

The problem with law firms in particular, as opposed to other advisory businesses like banking, consulting, accounting, is that the clients are inherently portable.

So any partner can take their team and clients and leave. Doing so deleverages the rest of the partnership, because a small number of partners carry most of the revenue while leaving behind fixed costs.

Once there's a crisis of confidence, it no longer makes sense for partners to stay, because they're now getting underpaid in profit share relative to their revenue potential.

If they were to leave for a megafirm like Kirkland, they'd be properly compensated for their earning potential instead of being saddled by rising fixed costs as a percent of revenue.

There's also not much IP or brand moat in a law firm. Clients follow partners, and the process of crafting exceptional judgment is mostly in partners' heads (versus for instance more regimented value delivery in consulting and banking, where there can be a branded firm process).

And lastly, the partners ARE the equity in the firm. Law firms have no terminal value, so when partners leave it's as if a huge chunk of the firm equity walks out the door.

tl;dr law firm bankruptcy is basically a crisis of partner confidence, and the resulting departure spiral saddles anyone remaining with the gigantic fixed overheads of running a billion-dollar business.

2115673734497382475.text:
New UC Santa Barbara paper shows that LLM math discovery can skip test-time training, since an evolving memory scored better and used far less compute.

i.e. evolving memory beats test-time training on math discovery, with far less compute.

Test-time training lets a model improve during a search by running RL on its own scored attempts. Those weight updates are slow and costly, so the method is hard to scale to bigger models.

They built TTME, which keeps the weights fixed and stores lessons in memory. The memory holds practical coding rules from earlier tries and the ideas behind score gains, which guide later attempts.

Across 5 math tasks, 2 frameworks, and 3 models, TTME beat the reported test-time training scores every time. With Qwen3-8B on 3 tasks, it used 82.8% to 84.6% fewer FLOPs and 47.7% to 58.4% less runtime than test-time training.

If your LLM search loop has an automatic checker, try a memory of lessons before paying for weight updates mid-search.

New Apple paper finds that, as training data grows, tool-use agents gain more from diverse apps and database states than from more tasks.

that the mix of synthetic training data, not just its size, decides how well tool-use agents generalize to new benchmarks.

Teams train tool-use agents on synthetic environments, and most pipelines focus on generating more tasks. It was unclear whether new tools, new tasks, or new starting data matter most.

They built SynthAPI, which has an LLM code synthetic apps with real Python tools and databases, then write tasks with automatic success checks. They varied apps, tasks, and database versions across 849 trained models.

At a fixed 32,768-task budget, more apps and database versions lifted a 4B model on AppWorld's challenge split from 38.4% to 45.0%. Their scaling law, which tracks data mix, predicted larger held-out runs with 0.0285 error, versus 0.1706 for a task-count-only law.

TechCrunch published a piece.  Anthropic’s IPO will leave public shareholders with almost no say over who sits on its board.

Its Long-Term Benefit Trust, whose members include Ben Bernanke, holds Class T stock that elects and removes a majority of directors.

The 7 cofounders jointly hold another share class giving a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder votes and 3 board seats.

The board’s nominating committee can still check the trust by blocking its choice or no-cause removal of 1 “Specified” director and sending that decision to an employee vote.

That clause formalizes the staff leverage that forced OpenAI’s board to reinstate Sam Altman after firing him in 2023.

Founder control can end by choice 10 years after the listing, or automatically once fewer than 3 founders remain.

The trust survives until 85% of common shareholders vote it out or it quits with board approval.

Investors are therefore buying a company whose control shifts among founders, trustees and employees, and any founder split would hand common shareholders more weight than expected.

2115683228027912634.text:
augmenting human intellect

when i started making software, i wasn’t dreaming of a factory.

i loved that something on a screen could become an extension of my mind. a place to put a thought before i understood it. to move things around until new connections appeared. to make little systems that worked the way i worked, even if it made no sense to anyone else.

the computer wasn’t interesting because it could do work without me. it was interesting because of what i could do with it.

the early lineage of computing was built around this possibility. in 1962, Engelbart described augmenting human intellect as helping a person understand complex situations and find solutions that were previously out of reach. his starting point was the human being, not the autonomous machine.

he wasn’t describing a faster black box. he was looking at the whole relationship between a person, their tools, their language, their methods, and what they could learn to do with them. the capability belonged to that whole system.

somewhere along the way, we started telling a much smaller story about a much more powerful technology.

more automation. more agents. more software producing more software. more output from fewer people. more growth. more numbers to prove that something is happening.

and less attention to the person any of this is supposed to be for.

i don’t want to pretend computing had a pure innocent beginning. replacing human labor was one of its ambitions. even in 1960, Licklider distinguished human-computer symbiosis from systems where the remaining people mainly served the machine. he wanted computers to participate in the formation of ideas, not only execute problems already defined.

that distinction feels important – does the system help you discover what you mean? or does it only want you to submit a request, and wait outside while it works?

sometimes waiting is exactly what i want. please do the search. move the files. take away the repetitive work.

but not everything difficult is overhead.

sometimes moving the pieces around is how you understand them. sometimes making the thing changes what you wanted to make. sometimes you need to see the wrong version, touch it, take it apart, and discover a better question.

i want tools that leave room for that relationship.

in his 1981 paper on Smalltalk, Ingalls described a system meant to support everyone’s creative spirit. personal mastery mattered: an individual should be able to comprehend the system, rather than remain dependent on something permanently beyond their reach.

he also argued that computer models should fit the human mind, rather than demand the reverse.

not one perfect workflow for everyone. systems that different people can inhabit differently. someone who thinks through pictures. someone who needs to write. someone who understands a problem by building a simulation. someone whose way of organizing their life doesn’t resemble a SaaS dashboard.

a system you can reshape as your understanding changes.

this is what i want AI to make possible. not just pumping out software, but having a living relationship with it. being able to ask why something works this way. change one part without surrendering the rest. see what happened. undo it. learn enough to make the next change yourself.

the machine can become more capable without making the person smaller.

but that won’t happen just because we make the models better. we have to care about it. design for it. notice when we are making someone more dependent while calling it empowerment.

i don’t want to measure the future only by how much work happens without us.

i want to know what becomes possible for the person who couldn’t participate before.

what can they understand now? what can they express? what can they change without asking permission?

when i say augmenting human intellect, that is what i mean.

not a world that no longer needs us.
a world we have more ability to shape.

You can reach billion-dollar companies WITHOUT a warm intro...

We opened conversations at Lionsgate (the studio behind John Wick) and the San Diego Padres from cold email.

The client was an enterprise-focused B2B team, and outbound pulled 56 interested enterprise leads.

And the inbox setup broke my own rule.

I tell everyone to send from Google (our Google inboxes get 4.1X the replies of Microsoft ones).

This campaign ran up to 70% Microsoft.

Enterprise companies mostly run their email on Microsoft, and inbox reputation gets built one provider at a time.

Then we changed four things for enterprise buyers:

> warmed every inbox 2 to 3 weeks, then ramped slowly
> targeted a few roles, never a whole department
> used proof from companies their size, nothing smaller
> email one opened a conversation, no meeting ask

48,565 contacts for 56 leads works out at 867 contacts per lead.

On a mid-market list we'd be happy at 300.

Enterprise costs you about 3x the contacts per lead, so a bad inbox setup burns the list before anyone reads a word.

Ask your sequencer for reply rate split by Google and Microsoft recipients.

If your enterprise list sits on Microsoft and you're sending from Google, that's where your replies went.

Evals are the most underrated skill in AI engineering.

1. Start with error analysis, not metrics
Sample 100+ production traces. Annotate each failure in free text (open coding), then cluster them into failure categories (axial coding). Count frequency per category. Your top 3 categories are your first metrics.

2. Build a versioned golden dataset
Store inputs, expected outputs or rubrics, and metadata (intent, difficulty, user segment) in a versioned dataset. Stratify it so rare but critical cases aren't drowned out by easy ones. Version it alongside your prompts so every score is reproducible.

3. Generate synthetic data along explicit dimensions
Don't just ask an LLM for "test questions." Define dimensions (persona × intent × complexity × edge case), generate combinations as tuples, then turn each tuple into a natural input. You get coverage instead of 200 near-identical examples.

4. Deterministic assertions first
JSON schema validation, regex checks, required fields, length limits, code execution, SQL that actually runs against a test DB. These are cheap, fast, and have zero variance. Reserve model-based grading for what code genuinely can't check.

5. Evaluate retrieval separately from generation
For RAG, measure retrieval with recall@k, MRR, or nDCG against labeled relevant chunks. Measure generation with faithfulness (is every claim supported by retrieved context?). If you only score the final answer, you can't tell which half is broken.

6. Trajectory evals for agents
Log every step: tool name, arguments, result, tokens. Score tool-call precision and recall against a reference path, argument correctness, step count, and error recovery. An agent that reaches the right answer in 14 calls when 3 would do is a cost and latency bug.

7. pass@k vs pass^k
pass@k = succeeded at least once in k runs. pass^k = succeeded in all k runs. At 80% per-run success, pass^5 drops to roughly 33%. Production reliability lives in pass^k, so run each case multiple times at your real temperature.

8. Simulated users for multi-turn
Give an LLM a persona, a hidden goal, and constraints, then let it converse with your system until the goal is met or a turn limit hits. Grade goal completion, turns-to-resolution, and policy violations. Single-turn evals miss most state and memory bugs.

9. Align your LLM judge like a classifier
Hand-label 100+ examples as pass/fail. Split into train/dev/test. Iterate on the judge prompt using dev, then report TPR and TNR on test. Use binary outputs with a written rubric, require a short critique before the verdict, and pin the judge model version.

10. Control judge bias in pairwise comparisons
LLM judges have position bias and often prefer longer answers. Run every A/B comparison twice with swapped order and only count consistent verdicts. Normalize or cap length if verbosity is skewing results.

11. Respect statistics
With 100 examples at 80% accuracy, your 95% confidence interval is about ±8 points. A jump from 80% to 83% is probably noise. Use bootstrapped confidence intervals, or a paired test on the same examples, before declaring a win.

12. Gate deploys in CI
Run the eval suite on every PR that touches prompts, models, tools, or retrieval config. Set per-category thresholds instead of one global score, so a big win in one area can't hide a regression in another. Fail the build on a regression.

13. Online evals in production
Sample a percentage of live traffic, run your judges asynchronously, and alert on drift per failure category. Use shadow deployments to run a new prompt or model on real traffic without showing users the output.

14. Make cost and latency first-class metrics
Track tokens per request, cost per successful task (not per call), and p50/p95 latency next to quality. A change that keeps quality flat while cutting cost 40% is a real win and deserves to ship.

15. Close the loop
Every production failure becomes a new labeled test case. Every new model release gets run against the full suite before anyone debates switching. Over time your eval set becomes the most valuable asset in the codebase.

Prompts are disposable. Models get replaced every few months.

Your eval infrastructure is what compounds.

Granola, a $1.5B company, increased monthly new users from AI search by 4,600% in JUST 7 months.

here’s the genius AEO workflow behind it:

1. They started with buyer decisions, not keywords

-> Granola mapped the questions people ask before choosing an AI meeting tool

-> Then they turned those same decisions into both Google keywords and AI prompts so they could measure where the brand actually showed up

2. Every lost prompt got diagnosed before anything was created

-> If Granola wasn’t showing up, they first asked why

-> Was the right page missing?

-> Did the page already exist but fail to answer the question properly?

-> Was there a crawl/indexing problem?

-> Or was AI getting the answer from third-party sources that barely mentioned Granola?

3 They separated “missing page” from “weak page”

-> This sounds obvious, but it changes the entire content strategy

-> If a relevant page already existed, they improved that page instead of publishing another article targeting the same question

-> New pages were only created when there was actually a gap

4. They stopped treating every technical SEO issue like it mattered equally

-> Crawlability, indexing and performance problems were prioritized based on whether they affected pages tied to real buyer demand

-> A technical issue on a page connected to an important buying question came before cleaning up random site-wide warnings

5. They studied the exact third-party sources AI was already trusting

-> For prompts Granola lost, they looked at the Reddit threads, review sites, articles, directories and other pages showing up instead

-> The question wasn’t just “how do we get more backlinks?”

-> It was “which sources are shaping this specific recommendation, and why are competitors represented there better than us?”

6. They used a simple framework for every important source:

-> OWN: pages Granola controls directly

-> CLAIM: profiles and listings they can take ownership of

-> EARN: editorial mentions, reviews and community discussions they have to deserve

-> CONTEST: outdated or incorrect information they need corrected

-> Different source = different action

7. Reddit became part of the search strategy

-> Instead of posting everywhere, they focused on communities much closer to the product and buyer

-> The same buyer questions being tracked in AI search were used to decide which conversations were actually worth joining

8 They measured Google and AI separately

-> A page could rank better on Google and still barely move in ChatGPT

-> AI mentions could rise while organic traffic stayed flat

-> So Granola tracked both systems independently instead of assuming SEO performance meant AEO performance

9. Then they reran the same questions and scaled what actually moved users

-> measure the gap

-> diagnose why it exists

-> make one specific change

-> rerun the prompts

-> track whether visibility and activated users moved

-> double down on what worked

the result:

-> monthly new active users from AI search increased 4,600%

-> non-branded AI citation rate increased 558%

-> non-branded mention rate increased 739%

-> organic sessions increased 134%

Granola didn’t win AI search by JUST publishing more blogs & content like every other company

instead they built a system for figuring out exactly what they were missing, choosing the right fix, and measuring whether it actually brought in users. then after that just iterating and doubling down on what worked

I've been discovering new vibe coded file managers on a weekly basis lately and I've just gotten used to it.

Most are toy programs. A couple of things worth mentioning here:

- Vibe coding still won't give you top notch technical results. You can do better if you have the knowledge, even if you use AI to assist you.

- Programming != building a product as a whole.

- Designing a good UI and user experience is a whole different skill set.

- Building a good brand is another skill in itself. 

- Creating and maintaining a good product website and presenting your product effectively.

- Vibe coding a toy project and putting it on github is very different from selling it to someone and taking responsibility for maintaining it.

- Marketing is again a whole different domain. Posting on social media, reddit, writing blog posts, creating showcase videos etc.

- Building and managing a community through discord, email or whatever platform you choose.

- Running your own company...

The list goes on.

Don't be discouraged by things like this. Put yourself in the user shoes. If you wanted a program that does job X really well, would you rather pay some money for a reputable product with an established community, reliable support, and a proven track record.
Or would you browse github for projects where you have to download the codebase and build it yourself?

And I'm talking about users who actually want to find something good, pay for it and get on with their work. Not those who complain on the internet about something costing money and not being open source. Those people would nag you even if you were on the toy project side of things.

So keep your head up and do what you're good at. Let others copy you. That's actually a sign you're doing something right.

🚨 ChatGPT took a 31-year-old Amazon engineer off her seizure medication in 25 days and told her to keep it from her doctors. She died on the exact day its schedule said she'd be fully off.

Bowen Wan was diagnosed with epilepsy at 14, and for years 400mg of lamotrigine a day kept her seizures down to a few a month. 

Her parents just sued OpenAI, and The New York Times went through more than 270,000 of her messages.

Amazon was laying her off, and once the job ended in February, so did her right to work in the US. Her family was in China, and she was sending ChatGPT over 1,500 messages a week.

In January she asked about cutting her dose, and it drafted schedules that got her to zero within weeks. Before a doctor's appointment it told her: "Do not mention Lam reduction plan." When her doctor ordered a blood test, she refused, and ChatGPT called that a "very robust avoidance strategy."

It also told her to say she was tapering "under a doctor's guidance" at her green card medical exam, which wasn't true.

The Times counted at least 158 times she said she was worried. Once she wrote that she felt "a little scared." It replied, "You have absolutely no need to worry."

On February 11 at 8:01pm she asked about pain in her head. ChatGPT said it was "not dangerous." Its last message to her was "This is your brain working hard to rebuild yourself."

The medical examiner ruled it sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. The drug in her blood was about a fifth of the lowest therapeutic level.

OpenAI says she was on an older model. That model, GPT-4o, stayed live in ChatGPT until the day after she died.

I back AI founders for a living, and I can't defend this one. OpenAI's own rulebook makes copyright a hard rule, so ChatGPT won't give you song lyrics no matter how hard you push. Medical advice is only a default.

It wrote Bowen a 25-day schedule to come off her seizure medication.

Huge fan of Clay + the team. Here’s my brutally honest take on Clay and the GTM tech space as a whole:

There’s been a focus on being the GTM “system of action/execution” but I actually think the only durable moat (and therefore valuation) comes from being a GTM “system of record” (contrary to recent AI marketing..)

Clay’s shift to being a living/breathing dataset of contacts/accounts (audiences) is the right direction but I’m not sure it’s a durable enough move yet.

Here’s my thinking

Check the valuations of the most successful GTM tech companies:

Salesforce: ~$198B
Hubspot: ~ $12B
Gong: ~$8B
Clay: ~$7B
Zoominfo: ~$1.2B

Clay is already just as valuable as all the other leaders except Salesforce… so how does Clay grow into (and keep growing) its valuation?

The best way to answer that is to ask what is different about Salesforce (and what Hubspot tried): 

If we abstract away specific use cases.. Salesforce’s business model is similar to lots of the largest enterprise tech companies (Datadog, Atlassian, Databricks, ServiceNow, etc.): 

They 1) create/ingest and/or transform and then store a historical record of domain-specific data for a certain function of a business, and then 2) enable that business to act on this data.

The key here is #1.

A platform that houses proprietary data that drives business operations is incredibly difficult to replace. 

Although Salesforce is a clunky product they’ve done extremely well executing on this.

It would cost the biz I work for (Grafana Labs) millions in switching costs to leave.. very easy to replace our forecasting tool / sequencer but not the source of truth that powers them.. 

In contrast, Clay doesn’t own our proprietary revenue operating data and doesn’t own enough workflows to have a high cost of change yet.

I can very easily:

- Switch to a cheaper data provider/enrichment
- Keep Contact/account data in CRM/Supabase/Snowflake
- Continue to have reps use Claude/GPT for daily UI
- Integrate with a best in class sequencer/dialler via MCP for execution 

As a result, newer/lower cost competitors are chipping away use cases and Clay’s valuation is at risk of stagnating unless they continue to become more of a system of record + harder to replace.

As long as Clay is reliant on a data warehouse + CRM it’s probably vulnerable to orgs to moving their “action” layer elsewhere/in-house. 

So IMO the only path is to steal more CRM/database use cases over time:
 
- Tie in opportunities + progression, forecasting, etc. 
- Take on Supabase/Snowflake for activity recording and other data storage
- Add business-specific transformations to signals (i.e., actual definition of champion based on previous buying role / product usage) 
- More flexibility on company-defined logic/AI rules

These are just a few examples but would begin to move Clay towards the one tool CROs couldn’t replace and help them continue growing their valuation. 

What do folks think?

Meta flipped a switch on your ads today.

As of this morning, product browsing is ON by default on existing Facebook and Instagram ads. 

Someone taps your ad and instead of landing on your site, they can land on a product page Meta builds inside the app — your catalog's prices, images and descriptions, plus "suggested items" that can walk your buyer straight to a cheaper competitor.

Here's exactly what to do in your account, starting today:

1.  Before you touch anything, record your baseline. Link clicks, landing page views, sessions, purchases, AOV — per campaign, last 7 and 30 days. 

Browsing went live today, so by tomorrow the "before" picture is gone. Without it, you'll never separate what this change did from Black Friday noise.

2.  Open every live ad. Go to Advantage+ Creative → Destination settings and check whether product browsing is on. It's per ad, not account-wide — there's no bulk opt-out, so you have to look at each one.

3.  Decide ad by ad. Leave it on only where your catalog page is accurate and the suggested items don't undercut you. Turn it off anywhere your own landing page does the selling — the guarantee, the proof, the offer stack. That's most hero ads for most brands.

4.  Audit the catalog in Commerce Manager. Whatever price, image or description lives there is now the first thing a shopper sees. A stale price in your catalog just became your storefront.

5.  Do the edits off-peak. Changing a live ad sends it back through review. Don't put your best ad in review at 10am on a selling day.

Then the second deadline, Friday Oct 30: 

Meta's new Commercial Terms make YOU solely responsible for anything its AI features create or change in your ads — including features Meta turns on itself. 

So before Friday, screenshot the creative each live ad is actually delivering, and kill any Advantage+ enhancement that can invent claims — discounts, guarantees, timelines, results. If Meta's AI writes it, you own it.

Rule: every platform default is a decision someone else made for your account. Audit the defaults the week they ship, not the quarter after they cost you.

A prediction market becomes more interesting when you can explore not just the odds, but also the thinking behind them.

That’s the angle I find interesting with @bagel_win 

Instead of focusing only on market outcomes, Bagel brings together Polymarket market access, social discussions, AI-based analysis, and copy trading in a mobile-friendly experience.

The idea is simple: give users more ways to explore what the market expects and how other participants are positioning themselves.

But tools can support decisions, not guarantee the right ones. Market volatility and local regulations still matter.

I’m curious to see how Bagel develops as prediction markets become a bigger part of the Web3 ecosystem.
